strengths: Comprehensive experimental validation across 8 benchmarks and multiple VLM architectures (3B-72B), demonstrating consistent improvements (51.8-108.8% on MindCube-Tiny)
Novel perspective on enabling intrinsic 3D reasoning in VLMs without requiring external tools at inference time, unlike methods such as Ego3D-VLM
Interpretability advantage through recovery of 3D point clouds from latent representations, providing visual explanations of the reasoning process
Well-designed two-stage training pipeline with clear motivation: supervised alignment (Stage 1) followed by outcome-driven RL refinement (Stage 2)
Thorough ablation studies examining latent size, token position, projector architecture, and reward components
Demonstrates strong generalization across different base VLM architectures and scales without model-specific tuning
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: combines established techniques (distillation, special tokens, GRPO) without introducing novel algorithmic contributions; individual components are straightforward

Misleading framing regarding external dependencies: the method fundamentally relies on VGGT (3D foundation model) for feature supervision during training, which contradicts the 'no external priors' claim; no analysis of sensitivity to choice of 3D model

Questionable quality of learned 3D representations: visualizations in Fig. 4 show crude, noisy point clouds; no quantitative evaluation metrics (e.g., Chamfer distance, 3D IoU) to validate reconstruction quality or geometric fidelity
Missing critical comparison with most relevant baseline (Mirage [79]), which is acknowledged as 'the most relevant mental model' but not directly evaluated in main results

Severe hyperparameter sensitivity demonstrated in Table 5: latent size of 12 is optimal; using 16 or 32 causes catastrophic performance drops (25.1% and 15.5% respectively), raising generalization concerns

Data construction concerns: only 10K training examples from MindCube; data generated via GPT-4o (proprietary model) with unexplained prompting strategy; no analysis of data quality or diversity impact
No computational cost analysis: training time, inference overhead, and memory requirements not reported; Stage 1 + Stage 2 cost compared to baselines unknown
Marginal improvements on certain sub-tasks (e.g., Travel Time in Ego3D-Bench shows minimal gains), and limited failure case analysis to understand failure modes

Evaluation scope limited to spatial reasoning tasks; unclear whether 3D thinking helps or harms performance on other VLM benchmarks; all benchmarks share similar characteristics (limited-view reasoning)

Contradictions in technical descriptions: limitations section states 3D latents are 'not autoregressively incorporated,' contradicting earlier framework descriptions; projector is frozen in Stage 2 without justification for why joint optimization was not attempted

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 8 benchmarks and multiple base VLMs (Qwen, InternVL, LLaVA) with consistent improvements, demonstrating broad applicability
Well-motivated two-stage training framework combining supervised feature alignment with outcome-based reinforcement learning
Provides extensive ablation studies on latent size, token position, projector design, and reward components
Clear presentation with informative figures and schematic illustrations of the methodology
Shows substantial improvements on MindCube-Tiny (51.8%-108.8%) and reasonable gains on Ego3D-Bench (18.1%-36.9%), with cross-dataset generalization demonstrated
Addresses an important problem in VLM spatial reasoning without requiring explicit external tools during inference (unlike Ego3D-VLM)
weaknesses: Overclaimed core contributions: the paper claims 'no 3D prior input' but VGGT features are used as direct supervision during Stage 1 training, making this a distilled rather than non-existent prior that deserves upfront acknowledgment

Limited technical novelty: the framework combines existing techniques (feature distillation, GRPO optimization, latent reasoning) without strong conceptual innovation beyond their application to spatial reasoning

Unsubstantiated central claim that VLM latents encode meaningful 3D geometric representations: no evidence that alignment with VGGT features produces 3D understanding rather than mere feature matching; point cloud visualizations are post-hoc reconstructions that don't prove latents inherently encode geometry

Insufficient ablation studies lack VGGT-agnostic alternatives (e.g., alignment with other 3D models, random features, or no alignment) to isolate whether improvements derive from the method or VGGT-specific properties

Inconsistent and suspicious performance patterns: (1) baseline VLM scores (e.g., Qwen2.5-3B at 33.2% on Rotation) seem unusually poor; (2) consistent weakness on Travel Time subtasks suggests method struggles with temporal/dynamic reasoning despite claims; (3) magnitude of gains vary dramatically across benchmarks without clear explanation

Missing critical technical clarity: unclear characterization of 3D latent tokens (dimension, structure, insertion strategy), vague terminology ('3D mentaling'), and unresolved autoregressive incorporation issues acknowledged but dismissed as future work

Incomplete experimental rigor: no statistical significance testing across multiple seeds, no computational cost analysis, limited cross-dataset generalization study, unfair comparison framing with respect to VGGT dependency, and no failure case analysis

Reproducibility concerns: code unavailable, VGGT model details and availability unclear, hyperparameter choices (e.g., latent size 12, λ₃D=0.1) lack justification, training time/compute not reported, and unclear whether synthetic CoT data will be released

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 8 benchmarks with multiple VLM architectures showing consistent substantial improvements (51.8-108.8% on MindCube-Tiny)
Practical approach requiring no external models at inference time and no explicit 3D annotations, with strong cross-dataset generalization
Well-motivated three-goal framework (3D-imaginable, annotation-free, intrinsic) clearly driving the methodology
Valuable interpretability through 3D latent visualization and point cloud recovery from learned representations
Thorough ablation studies on latent size, token positioning, projector design, and reward components demonstrating careful engineering
Consistent outperformance of recent SOTA methods (SpatialLadder-3B +21.8%, VILASR-7B +33.7%) without external inference tools
Good generalization to unseen datasets (trained on MindCube, strong performance on Ego3D-Bench)
weaknesses: Moderate technical novelty: Stage 1 uses standard distillation and Stage 2 applies existing GRPO with simple reward design; projector is just an MLP
Conceptual clarity issues: '3D thinking' is primarily alignment to VGGT features rather than intrinsic 3D understanding; semantic meaning of '3D latents' is opaque
Contradicts 'intrinsic' claim (G3): heavily depends on VGGT during training and GPT-4o for data generation, creating external dependencies despite inference-time claims
Limited analysis of learned representations: no ablation isolating 3D component from additional parameters; weaker rotation improvements suggest dynamic spatial imagination is underexplored
Modest and inconsistent Stage 2 RL gains (19.9% on MindCube-Tiny vs 8.8% on Ego3D-Bench) with some subtasks showing performance decreases, raising stability concerns
Hyperparameter sensitivity and lack of justification: latent size drops from 62.7% to 25.1% (size 32), λ parameters set arbitrarily without ablation
Reproducibility concerns: depends on closed-source GPT-4o for CoT generation and VGGT, with sparse architectural details for the projector
Evaluation concerns: weak baseline (Qwen2.5-VL-3B: 33.2% on MindCube-Tiny) suggests possible dataset fitting; improvements on single-image tasks are modest relative to multi-view gains
Missing exploration: Why VGGT specifically? No analysis of whether alternative 3D models would work or what makes VGGT particularly suitable
Incomplete related work comparison: Mirage is identified as most relevant but receives only brief discussion with no direct equivalent-setting comparisons

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing real limitations of text-only spatial reasoning in VLMs, with compelling connection to human 3D cognitive abilities
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 8+ diverse benchmarks with consistent improvements over strong baselines including recent VLMs (Qwen2.5-VL, LLaVA-OneVision)
Thoughtful two-stage training framework that elegantly combines supervised learning with outcome-based reinforcement learning, reducing dependence on dense annotations
Extensive ablation studies (Tables 3-6, 11) systematically validating design choices for latent size, token positioning, projector configuration, and loss components
Interpretable approach with visualizations of reconstructed 3D point clouds that provide transparency into learned representations during reasoning
Practical data generation strategy creating synthetic CoT data from MindCube without requiring additional manual annotation
Clear presentation with effective framework visualization (Figure 2) and logical paper organization
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty - primarily an engineering combination of existing techniques (VLMs, standard 3D foundation models, conventional reward formulations) with no novel algorithmic contributions

Insufficient evidence that true 3D spatial reasoning is learned rather than pattern memorization: simple alignment loss (Eq. 5), noisy point cloud visualizations, and lack of rigorous analysis of learned representations
Evaluation scope narrowly confined to MindCube-derived spatial QA tasks without real-world spatial reasoning tasks, limiting claims about generalization beyond benchmark-specific improvements

Heavy dependence on synthetic data from MindCube and specific VGGT features raises reproducibility and generalization concerns; data generation via GPT-4.1 lacks detail on success rates and quality validation

Missing critical analyses: no statistical significance testing, no inference time/memory overhead comparison, no ablation isolating Stage 2's contribution, and modest improvements in some cases (88.9% vs. 83.2%)
Stage 2 (reinforcement learning) contribution unclear - Table 11 ablation doesn't isolate Stage 2's value, and many improvements appear achievable with Stage 1 alone
Limited failure analysis with only one case shown; no systematic characterization of failure modes or guidance for addressing identified limitations
Unclear if improvements stem from 3D reasoning or increased model capacity from adding 3D tokens - no comparison with equivalent capacity baseline without 3D components
High computational cost (21.84h + 12.85h on H100) and complex two-stage training with multiple hyperparameter sets (6 configurations mentioned) limit practical adoption without efficiency analysis
No cross-dataset generalization experiments, evaluation on real images, or justification of why VGGT features are optimal for 3D reasoning

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 8+ diverse benchmarks with consistent evaluation protocol
Strong empirical improvements on MindCube-Tiny dataset (88.9% improvement in Stage 1)
Well-documented data generation process with detailed hyperparameters supporting reproducibility
Thorough ablation studies examining latent size, projector configurations, reward designs, and training strategies
Effective qualitative visualizations (Figures 10-16) showing reasoning processes and 3D reconstruction from limited views
Good generalization across multiple VLM architectures (Qwen2.5-VL, LLaVA, InternVL families)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty—primarily engineering existing components (VGGT, standard projectors, GRPO) without significant methodological innovation; core 3D alignment is straightforward L2 distance
Misleading 'annotation-free' framing—method heavily depends on VGGT (trained with extensive annotations), uses manual CoT curation via GPT-4, and relies on 10K hand-curated MindCube samples
Inconsistent and often marginal improvements: VSI-Bench shows 0.3% gain; MMSI-Bench shows modest 3.3% improvement; Stage 2 adds only 2% on MindCube-Tiny (73.2→75.2%)
Critical dependency on VGGT as 3D foundation model without robustness analysis or evaluation using alternative 3D representations; framework utility unclear if VGGT unavailable

Unfair baseline comparisons: many baselines use older VLM architectures (Qwen2.5-VL-3B, LLaVA-1.5); no comparison with recent state-of-the-art VLMs; mixing single-image vs. multi-view results clouds conclusions

Limited evaluation diversity: all experiments on indoor scenes or controlled settings; generalization relies primarily on VGGT transfer; no evaluation on truly diverse out-of-distribution real-world scenarios

Single failure case presented (Section 14.2) attributes error to 'sparse views causing inaccurate reconstruction'—contradicts core claim of handling limited views effectively; lacks systematic failure mode analysis

Stage 2 RL justification weak: modest improvements (2-3% absolute) do not clearly justify 12.85h additional training time; multi-component reward design introduced without rigorous justification; no ablation on individual reward necessity

Insufficient technical depth: projector is basic MLP/pooling; no novel RL formulation; frozen projector in Stage 2 unexplained; direct projection achieves 74.1% vs. complex method at 75.2% (only 1.1% difference)

Incomplete analysis: no study of minimum CoT data requirements; missing error bars and variance reporting; MRA metric poorly explained; no systematic error type analysis; computational cost comparison with baselines absent

strengths: Novel framework enabling VLMs to perform spatial reasoning by integrating 3D mental representations during thinking processes, addressing genuine limitations in multimodal reasoning
Impressive empirical results with consistent improvements across 8 diverse benchmarks (e.g., 88.9% improvement on MindCube-Tiny from 62.7 to 73.2 accuracy)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation including thorough ablation studies, multiple baseline comparisons, and analysis across different VLM architectures (Qwen2.5-VL, LLaVA-OneVision, InternVL)
Technically sound two-stage training methodology that cleverly balances supervised learning with outcome-based reinforcement learning, avoiding dense 3D annotation requirements in stage 2
Strong reproducibility with clear methodology, detailed hyperparameters, reasonable computational requirements (21.84h + 12.85h on single H100), and promised code release
Effective visualization of 3D mental representations and spatial reasoning process, demonstrating the interpretability of the approach
Good generalization across different spatial reasoning scenarios and VLM architectures, indicating broad applicability
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty—framework primarily combines existing components (VLMs, VGGT projector, 3D foundation models) with main contribution being the training strategy rather than novel architecture design

Understated dependency on pre-trained 3D foundation model (VGGT)—the 'annotation-free' claim applies only to stage 2, while the method's performance is fundamentally bounded by foundation model quality, and sensitivity analysis is missing
Stage 1 still requires constructing specialized CoT dataset with 10,000 samples using GPT-4.1 for synthetic generation, partially undermining the 'annotation-free' positioning
Insufficient failure analysis with only one failure case (Figure 17) and limited systematic exploration of failure modes, particularly for sparse viewpoints or challenging scene types

Evaluation predominantly focused on visual question answering with limited evidence of effectiveness on other spatial reasoning tasks (navigation, manipulation, etc.) beyond multi-view scene understanding
Missing inference-time cost analysis—no discussion of computational overhead during 3D feature generation and no latency comparison with baselines
Unexplored ablation on stage 1 data quantity—performance scaling with different amounts of CoT data (currently fixed at 10,000) is not investigated

Incomplete clarity on technical details including justification for VGGT choice over alternatives, sensitivity to hyperparameter selection (λ₁, λ₂, λ₃), and what 3D properties the model actually learns to represent
Limited analysis of why some competitive baselines (e.g., Spatial-Ladder with 56.4 performance) perform comparably, making it unclear what drives improvements
